facts.where: Etymology under Abracadabrella gen. nov. (about p. 627)

facts.t: Abracadabrella looks like the flat-bodied Afraflacilla-Pseudicius group in shape and colour but lacks their stridulatory organs.

facts.t: Male-male fights in Bavia aericeps are ferocious, with rivals often upended and stunned.

facts.t: Cocalus gibbosus stalks across other spiders' webs without sticking to their glue, yet it makes no deceptive vibrations, unlike Portia.

facts.checked: read abstract via Consensus search; DOI from Crossref metadata

facts.t: Cocalus gibbosus moults and lays eggs on silk sheets spun against tree trunks, never building a typical enclosed salticid nest.

facts.kp: moulted and oviposited on silk sheets spun against tree trunks ... never built an enclosing nest
facts.checked: read abstract via Consensus search; DOI from Crossref metadata

facts.t: Unlike seven web-signalling spartaeines, Cocalus gibbosus failed a trial-and-error escape test from an island in water.

facts.checked: read abstract via Consensus search; DOI from Crossref metadata

facts.t: In lab tests, Cocalus stalking a web spider moved farther while simulated wind or struggling prey shook the web, masking its approach.

facts.kp: moved significantly farther during intervals when disturbances ... were present
facts.checked: read abstract via Consensus search; DOI from Crossref metadata
facts.note: Lab study with lures; the abstract names genera, not species (probably C. gibbosus, the Australian Cocalus this group studied). Also applies to Cyrba.

facts.t: Coccorchestes ferreus, described in 1984 from one female collected in 1949, was the first of this New Guinea genus found in Australia.

facts.note: Holotype from Cape York Peninsula, Qld (exact locality omitted). Griswold suggested it is a remnant of a Pleistocene biota shared with New Guinea.

facts.t: Female Coccorchestes ferreus are about 3 mm long, with a pitted, armoured carapace and a shiny, hairless shield over the abdomen.
facts.cite: Griswold CE (1984) Coccorchestes Thorell newly described from Australia (Araneae: Salticidae). Bull Br Arachnol Soc 6: 147-148
facts.kp: carapace armoured with oval pits ... shiny, brown scutum; scutum smooth, without setae ... total length = 3.0

facts.t: Cosmophasis bitaeniata eats green tree ant larvae and mimics the ants' cuticular hydrocarbons; major workers ignored its cuticle extracts.
facts.cite: Allan RA, Capon RJ, Brown WV, Elgar MA (2002) Mimicry of host cuticular hydrocarbons by salticid spider Cosmophasis bitaeniata that preys on larvae of tree ants Oecophylla smaragdina. J Chem Ecol 28: 835-848
facts.kp: qualitative chemical mimicry of ants by C. bitaeniata allows the spiders to avoid detection
facts.note: Host ant: Oecophylla smaragdina.

facts.t: Cosmophasis bitaeniata gets its ant-like scent by eating green ant larvae, so its chemical profile matches the colony it fed from.
facts.cite: Elgar MA, Allan RA (2004) Predatory spider mimics acquire colony-specific cuticular hydrocarbons from their ant model prey. Naturwissenschaften 91: 143-147
facts.kp: the spider acquires the cuticular hydrocarbons by eating the ant larvae
facts.note: Profile depends on the colony of origin of the larval prey, not the spider's parentage; contact with adult ants is not the source.

facts.t: In Cosmophasis umbratica, males reflect UV while females glow green under UV; blocking either signal disrupted courtship.
facts.cite: Lim MLM, Land MF, Li D (2007) Sex-specific UV and fluorescence signals in jumping spiders. Science 315: 481
facts.kp: UV reflectance and UV-induced green fluorescence restricted to males and females, respectively
facts.note: Studied in Singapore.

facts.t: Male Cosmophasis umbratica get UV colour from scales built as a chitin-air-chitin sandwich, which adds a second reflection peak near 385 nm.
facts.cite: Land MF, Horwood J, Lim MLM, Li D (2007) Optics of the ultraviolet reflecting scales of a jumping spider. Proc R Soc B 274: 1583-1589
facts.kp: chitin-air-chitin sandwich ... produces a second reflectance peak at approximately 385 nm

facts.t: Portia labiata, a spider-eating salticid, chose UV-reflecting male Cosmophasis umbratica over males with their UV filtered out.
facts.cite: Bulbert MW, O'Hanlon JC, Zappettini S, Zhang S, Li D (2015) Sexually selected UV signals in the tropical ornate jumping spider, Cosmophasis umbratica may incur costs from predation. Ecology and Evolution 5: 914-920
facts.kp: Portia labiata exhibited a strong bias toward UV+ individuals

facts.t: Infrared video showed Cyrba algerina from Azerbaijan catching prey in complete darkness.
facts.cite: Guseinov EF, Cerveira AM, Jackson RR (2004) The predatory strategy, natural diet, and life cycle of Cyrba algerina, an araneophagic jumping spider (Salticidae: Spartaeinae) from Azerbaijan. NZ J Zool 31: 291-303

facts.t: Evarcha culicivora, an East African species, feeds indirectly on vertebrate blood by choosing blood-fed female mosquitoes as prey.

facts.kp: feeds indirectly on vertebrate blood by choosing as preferred prey female mosquitoes

facts.t: In Evarcha culicivora, eating blood-fed mosquitoes gives a spider an odour that makes it more attractive to the opposite sex.

facts.t: Evarcha culicivora is drawn to human odour: in tests, adults and juveniles stayed longer near previously worn socks than unworn ones.
facts.cite: Cross FR, Jackson RR (2011) Olfaction-based anthropophily in a mosquito-specialist predator. Biology Letters 7: 510-512

facts.t: Male Evarcha culicivora have bright red faces; males facing a mirror image with the red hidden by eyeliner escalated less.

facts.t: Some Evarcha arcuata rest at night hanging from a single silk thread fixed to vegetation overhead, rather than in a silk retreat.

facts.t: Of 1115 field prey records for Evarcha culicivora, 80% were mosquitoes, most of them females.

facts.note: Alternative E. culicivora facts if wanted: innate attraction to Lantana camara volatiles (Nelson et al. 2012 J Chem Ecol 38:1081, doi 10.1007/s10886-012-0175-x); juveniles drink nectar (Carvell et al. 2015 R Soc Open Sci, doi 10.1098/rsos.140426).

facts.t: A Sri Lankan Gelotia invades other spiders' webs, deceives the owner with specialised vibrations, then eats it.

facts.note: Undescribed species; first behavioural data for the genus.

facts.t: Like Portia, a Sri Lankan Gelotia hangs up a dead leaf on which it rests and lays its eggs.
facts.cite: Jackson RR (1990) Predatory and silk utilisation behaviour of Gelotia sp. indet. (Araneae: Salticidae: Spartaeinae), a web-invading aggressive mimic from Sri Lanka. NZ J Zool 17: 475-482
facts.kp: Gelotia, like Portia, hung up a dead leaf on which to rest and oviposit
facts.checked: read abstract via Consensus search; DOI from Crossref metadata

facts.t: Grayenulla, named for arachnologist Michael Gray, is known from dry semi-desert inland Queensland and WA, mostly from pitfall traps.
facts.cite: Zabka M (1992) Salticidae (Arachnida: Araneae) from Oriental, Australian and Pacific Regions, VII. Paraplatoides and Grayenulla - new genera from Australia and New Caledonia. Records of the Australian Museum 44: 165-183
facts.where: Etymology and 'Biology and distribution' of Grayenulla, p. 174-176
facts.kp: collected in dry, semidesert inland regions of Queensland and Western Australia, mostly by pitfall traps
facts.checked: read full text (Australian Museum PDF scan, text layer extracted)
facts.note: Paper adds that no specimens had been found in coastal Australia.

facts.t: Grayenulla has three strong bristles jutting from the middle of the clypeus, and its third legs are the longest.
facts.cite: Zabka M (1992) Salticidae (Arachnida: Araneae) from Oriental, Australian and Pacific Regions, VII. Paraplatoides and Grayenulla - new genera from Australia and New Caledonia. Records of the Australian Museum 44: 165-183
facts.where: Diagnosis and description of Grayenulla, p. 175
facts.kp: 3 central bristles on clypeus ... Third legs distinctly the longest
facts.checked: read full text (Australian Museum PDF scan, text layer extracted)

facts.t: Hasarius adansoni gauges depth from blur: one green-sensitive retinal layer always gets a defocused image; light colour alters its jumps.
facts.cite: Nagata T, Koyanagi M, Tsukamoto H, et al. (2012) Depth perception from image defocus in a jumping spider. Science 335: 469-471
facts.where: abstract (mechanism); species named in Nagata et al. 2019 J Comp Neurol 527:1348 abstract and press coverage
facts.kp: the second-deepest layer always receives defocused images, which contain depth information
facts.checked: read abstract on PubMed (PMID 22282813); species confirmed via Nagata et al. 2019 abstract (PMID 30458068) and phys.org report
facts.note: Press reports (phys.org, Scientific American) say jumps under red light fell short; that detail is not in the abstract.

facts.t: Hasarius adansoni uses its dragline mid-jump to correct body pitch; without silk, spiders landing upright slipped or tumbled.
facts.cite: Chen YK, Liao CP, Tsai FY, Chi KJ (2013) More than a safety line: jump-stabilizing silk of salticids. J R Soc Interface 10: 20130572
facts.kp: Without silk, upright-landing spiders would slip or even tumble

facts.t: Hasarius adansoni learned to avoid coloured papers paired with heat, telling blue, green, yellow and red apart, apparently by hue.
facts.cite: Nakamura T, Yamashita S (2000) Learning and discrimination of colored papers in jumping spiders (Araneae, Salticidae). J Comp Physiol A 186: 897-901
facts.kp: jumping spiders can discriminate the blue, green, yellow and red papers by their hue
facts.note: Authors note brightness may also be used alongside hue.

facts.t: Tested in darkness, Helpis minitabunda kept a roughly straight path through a maze by alternating left and right turns.
facts.cite: Taylor PW (1995) Jumping spiders alternate turns in the absence of visual cues. International Journal of Comparative Psychology 8(2)
facts.kp: each species turned in the direction opposite to the forced turn
facts.checked: read abstract via Consensus search; DOI from Crossref metadata; year and issue from eScholarship listing
facts.note: Also shown for Portia fimbriata, Trite auricoma and Trite planiceps; author suggests proprioception. Crossref gives 2012 (online posting date).

facts.t: Helpis minitabunda exposed to field doses of the insecticide imidacloprid took over twice as long to handle prey and killed fewer.
facts.cite: Rajan-Sheela R, Wignall A (2026) The neonicotinoid imidacloprid impairs the predatory performance and functional response of the jumping spider Helpis minitabunda. J Econ Entomol
facts.kp: treated spiders showed more than double the handling time compared to controls
facts.note: Applied/ecotox study; include only if wanted.

facts.t: In a New Zealand Holoplatys, well-fed spiders never killed displaying conspecifics but often ate ones that failed to display.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Harding DP (1982) Intraspecific interactions of Holoplatys sp. indet., a New Zealand jumping spider (Araneae: Salticidae). New Zealand J Zool 9: 487-510
facts.kp: well fed spiders never killed displaying conspecifics, they frequently killed and ate ones that failed
facts.checked: abstract reconstructed from OpenAlex record; citation from Crossref
facts.note: Species unidentified (Holoplatys sp. indet.). Starved spiders often killed even displaying conspecifics; authors propose display protects against cannibalism.

facts.t: A New Zealand Holoplatys has about 27 major displays, a repertoire the authors called unusually large and complex for a salticid.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Harding DP (1982) Intraspecific interactions of Holoplatys sp. indet., a New Zealand jumping spider (Araneae: Salticidae). New Zealand J Zool 9: 487-510
facts.kp: Approximately 27 major displays occur
facts.note: Species unidentified (Holoplatys sp. indet.). Males also have three mating tactics, as in Mopsus mormon.

facts.t: Jacksonoides queenslandicus is the salticid Portia fimbriata most often eats in Queensland; Portia knows it partly by its big front eyes.
facts.cite: Harland DP, Jackson RR (2000) Cues by which Portia fimbriata, an araneophagic jumping spider, distinguishes jumping-spider prey from other prey. J Exp Biol 203: 3485-3494
facts.kp: Jacksonoides queenslandicus ... the salticid species on which it most commonly preys
facts.note: Portia used cryptic stalking only when the lure's large anterior median eyes were visible. 'Big front eyes' = anterior median eyes.

facts.t: Jacksonoides queenslandicus catches prey in the webs of other spiders, and females were seen eating each other's eggs.
facts.cite: Jackson RR (1988) The biology of Jacksonoides queenslandica, a jumping spider (Araneae: Salticidae) from Queensland: intraspecific interactions, web-invasion, predators, and prey. New Zealand J Zool 15: 1-37
facts.kp: captured prey in webs of other spiders ... Females ate each other's eggs.
facts.note: Paper used the spelling J. queenslandica; current name J. queenslandicus Wanless, 1988 (WSC). Its nests resemble both sheet-like lyssomanine nests and tubular nests.

facts.t: Male Jotus remus wave a bristly paddle on leg III over the edge of a leaf to lure a female on the far side; it is not used face to face.
facts.cite: Otto JC, Hill DE (2016) Males of a new species of Jotus from Australia wave a paddle-shaped lure to solicit nearby females (Araneae: Salticidae: Euophryini). Peckhamia 133.1: 1-39
facts.where: species treatment (Plazi XML of the paper)
facts.kp: only used to attract the attention of a female on the opposite side of a leaf or stem
facts.checked: read the Jotus remus treatment text via Plazi (tb.plazi.org/GgServer/xml/495C87F2371E8032FD99F9A101AB012A); citation from Plazi/Zenodo record
facts.note: Females often stalked and attacked the paddle; the authors suggest those females had mated before, while a courted virgin did not attack it.

facts.t: Jotus remus is named from the Latin for oar, after the flat paddle of long setae at the end of each male third leg.
facts.cite: Otto JC, Hill DE (2016) Males of a new species of Jotus from Australia wave a paddle-shaped lure to solicit nearby females (Araneae: Salticidae: Euophryini). Peckhamia 133.1: 1-39
facts.kp: English translation oar or paddle ... a flat 'paddle' comprised of long setae
facts.checked: read the etymology in the Plazi treatment XML
facts.note: Use only one of the two Jotus remus facts on a card if space is tight; the lure fact is stronger.

facts.t: Adult Judalana lutea resemble the ant Opisthopsis rufithorax, but its hatchlings look like small black ants until a few moults later.
facts.cite: Rix MG (1999) A new genus and species of ant-mimicking jumping spider (Araneae: Salticidae) from southeast Queensland, with notes on its biology. Mem Queensl Mus 43(2): 827-832
facts.where: Biology and Life history, pp. 827 and 829
facts.kp: Newly hatched juveniles are very similar in appearance to common small black ants
facts.note: Males resemble the ant more than females do. No specimen was seen to eat ants; captives took tiny flies.

facts.t: A Judalana lutea female guards her orange eggs inside a folded leaf until they hatch, after which she dies.
facts.cite: Rix MG (1999) A new genus and species of ant-mimicking jumping spider (Araneae: Salticidae) from southeast Queensland, with notes on its biology. Mem Queensl Mus 43(2): 827-832
facts.kp: A female with her egg sac stayed with it until the eggs hatched, after which she died.
facts.note: About 11-14 eggs per sac; based on observation of a female (singular) in the source, so 'a female' rather than a general rule. Mainly on Acacia bushes.

facts.t: Judalana was named by its describer, Michael Rix, after his parents, Judy and Alan.
facts.cite: Rix MG (1999) A new genus and species of ant-mimicking jumping spider (Araneae: Salticidae) from southeast Queensland, with notes on its biology. Mem Queensl Mus 43(2): 827-832
facts.kp: ETYMOLOGY. For my parents, Judy and Alan.
facts.note: Males have frontal horns on the chelicerae, unique among related Australian ant mimics (diagnosis).

facts.t: Ligonipes illustris belongs to Australia's golden mimicry complex: at least 140 gold-bodied, ant-like species from four arthropod orders.
facts.cite: Pekar S, Petrakova L, Bulbert MW, Whiting MJ, Herberstein ME (2017) The golden mimicry complex uses a wide spectrum of defence to deter a community of predators. eLife 6: e22089
facts.where: abstract; species listed in Table 1 (mimic species of the golden complex)
facts.kp: at least 140 different putative mimics from four arthropod orders
facts.checked: read abstract on PubMed (PMID 28170317); Table 1 entry confirmed in Europe PMC full text (PMC5295815)
facts.note: Listed as a putative mimic only; Ligonipes was not used in the predator trials. Golden ant models include Polyrhachis species.

facts.t: Maddisonia, named for salticid authority Wayne Maddison, holds tiny spiders under 3 mm long with a large, corkscrew-like embolus.
facts.cite: Zabka M (2014) Maddisonia, a new jumping spider genus from Australia (Arachnida: Araneae: Salticidae). Rec Aust Mus 66(4): 217-223
facts.kp: The name is proposed for Prof. Wayne Maddison ... Embolus large, cork-screw-like
facts.note: Description: 'Spiders below 3 mm long.' Known from Qld, NSW and WA.

facts.t: Maddisonia berbekai honours Polish mountaineer Maciej Berbeka, who died in 2013 during a pioneering winter ascent of Broad Peak.
facts.cite: Zabka M (2014) Maddisonia, a new jumping spider genus from Australia (Arachnida: Araneae: Salticidae). Rec Aust Mus 66(4): 217-223
facts.kp: who died during a pioneering winter ascent of Broad Peak in Karakoram
facts.note: Known from Western Australia (holotype from a pitfall trap). The other species honour Barry Richardson and Robert Whyte.

facts.t: Super-black patches on male Maratus speciosus and M. karrie reflect under 0.5% of light, helped by tightly packed cuticular microlens bumps.
facts.cite: McCoy DE, McCoy VE, Mandsberg NK, Shneidman AV, Aizenberg J, Prum RO, Haig D (2019) Structurally assisted super black in colourful peacock spiders. Proc R Soc B 286: 20190589
facts.kp: super black regions reflect less than 0.5% of light ... owing to microscale structures
facts.note: M. karrie also has black brush-like scales on top of the bumps. Authors propose super black makes adjacent colours look brighter, convergent with birds of paradise.

facts.t: The rainbow scales of Maratus robinsoni and M. chrysomelas carry nanogratings on curved surfaces that split light into the full spectrum.
facts.cite: Hsiung B-K, Siddique RH, Stavenga DG, Otto JC, Allen MC, Liu Y, Lu Y-F, Deheyn DD, Shawkey MD, Blackledge TA (2017) Rainbow peacock spiders inspire miniature super-iridescent optics. Nat Commun 8: 2278
facts.kp: tiny structured scales ... reflect the full visual spectrum ... 2D nanogratings on microscale 3D convex surfaces
facts.note: Scales about 40 x 10 micrometres; the curved gratings have at least twice the resolving power of a flat grating of the same period.

facts.t: Maratus splendens has the fastest jump acceleration yet measured in a jumping spider; leg III powers the jump and features in courtship.
facts.cite: Narendra A, Seibel A, Ramirez-Esquivel F, Joshi P, McLean DJ, Robledo-Ospina L, Rao D (2025) Sexual dimorphism in jump kinematics and choreography in peacock spiders. J Exp Biol 228(3): jeb249416
facts.kp: peacock spiders exhibited the fastest acceleration among all known jumping spiders
facts.note: Filmed at 5000 frames/s; males took off faster and at steeper angles than females. 'Fastest' is among jumping spiders measured to date.

facts.t: Male Maratus volans pair their dance with substrate vibrations; mating success depended on both the visual and the vibratory display.
facts.cite: Girard MB, Elias DO, Kasumovic MM (2015) Female preference for multi-modal courtship: multiple signals are important for male mating success in peacock spiders. Proc R Soc B 282: 20152222
facts.kp: success contingent upon a combination of visual and vibratory displays
facts.checked: read abstract on PubMed (PMID 26631566); vibratory signals first described in Girard, Kasumovic & Elias 2011 PLoS ONE 6: e25390 (doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0025390), abstract read
facts.note: Vibrations recorded by laser vibrometry.

facts.t: In Maratus splendens the blue scales have no pigment and are coloured by structure, while its white, cream and red scales are pigmentary.
facts.cite: Stavenga DG, Otto JC, Wilts BD (2016) Splendid coloration of the peacock spider Maratus splendens. J R Soc Interface 13: 20160437
facts.kp: Blue scales are unpigmented and have a structural colour
facts.note: The blue comes from two ridged chitin layers separated by an air gap, with a filament array the authors call a novel structural colour system.

facts.t: Maratus griseus tracked glossy moving targets less precisely than matte ones, and its attack jumps at glossy targets were far less accurate.
facts.cite: Franklin AM, Brown MR, Willmott NJ (2024) Glossiness disrupts predator localisation of moving prey. Curr Biol 34(22): R1131-R1132
facts.kp: jumping spider attack jumps were substantially less accurate towards glossy prey
facts.note: Here Maratus is the predator, used as a model to test prey glossiness; effect independent of target colour (green or grey).

facts.t: Megaloastia mainae spends most of its time on downward-facing surfaces of large rocks; its long legs may suit rapid running upside down.
facts.cite: Soley FG, McGinley RH, Collins SR, Taylor PW (2016) Natural history observations and predatory behaviour of a long-legged jumping spider, Megaloastia mainae (Araneae: Salticidae). New Zealand J Zool 43(1): 65-83
facts.kp: spends most of its time on downward-facing horizontal surfaces of large rocks
facts.checked: abstract text reconstructed from OpenAlex record; sentences on rock surfaces and legs quoted verbatim
facts.note: Known from Kimberley rock escarpments, WA. Legs: 'may be the result of selection for rapid locomotion in inverted environments.' No evidence it builds a prey-capture web or uses its nest to hunt, contrary to earlier reports.

facts.t: Menemerus semilimbatus was the first invertebrate shown to tell biological motion from random motion in point-light displays.
facts.cite: De Agrò M, Rößler DC, Kim K, Shamble PS (2021) Perception of biological motion by jumping spiders. PLoS Biol 19(7): e3001172
facts.kp: first demonstration of biological motion recognition in an invertebrate
facts.checked: read abstract on PubMed (PMID 34264925); species confirmed on journals.plos.org methods
facts.note: Spiders on a treadmill turned preferentially toward the random display, not the biological one.

facts.t: With other eyes masked, Menemerus semilimbatus told biological from random motion only when its anterior lateral eyes could see.
facts.cite: De Agrò M, Rößler DC, Shamble PS (2024) Eye-specific detection and a multi-eye integration model of biological motion perception. J Exp Biol 227(12): jeb247061
facts.kp: able to discriminate stimuli only when the anterior lateral eyes were unblocked
facts.checked: read abstract on PubMed (PMID 38752337); species confirmed in Europe PMC full text (PMC11418026)
facts.note: Each eye pair tested alone; in this study spiders preferred the biological stimulus, unlike in 2021.

facts.t: Menemerus females guarding hatchlings abandoned them more often when they saw ants or ant-like Myrmarachne melanotarsa, a brood predator.
facts.cite: Nelson XJ, Jackson RR (2009) Aggressive use of Batesian mimicry by an ant-like jumping spider. Biol Lett 5: 755-757
facts.kp: When seeing ants or ant mimics, Menemerus females abandoned their broods more frequently
facts.note: Species not identified (Menemerus sp., East Africa). Pairs with the Myrmarachne melanotarsa fact.

facts.t: Mopsus mormon males court females outside nests visually but inside nests by non-visual signals, and cohabit beside subadult females.
facts.cite: Jackson RR (1983) The biology of Mopsus mormon, a jumping spider (Araneae: Salticidae) from Queensland: intraspecific interactions. Aust J Zool 31: 39-53
facts.kp: then spin an adjacent silken chamber and cohabit
facts.checked: abstract reconstructed from OpenAlex record (publisher page would not load); title/pages from Crossref
facts.note: Three mating tactics depending on female maturity and location; the paper calls the display repertoire unusually large and complex for a salticid.

facts.t: Myrmaplata plataleoides mimics weaver ants but avoids touching them; a group of its model ants was photographed killing a female in India.
facts.cite: Ramachandra P, Hill DE (2018) Predation by the weaver ant Oecophylla smaragdina (Hymenoptera: Formicidae: Formicinae) on its mimic jumping spider Myrmarachne plataleoides. Peckhamia 174.1: 1-8
facts.kp: cooperative attack on a female M. plataleoides by a group of these ants
facts.checked: read the PDF text (summary and introduction)
facts.note: Paper uses Myrmarachne plataleoides and notes Proszynski (2016) made it type of Myrmaplata; check WSC for the currently accepted combination. Only one earlier report of such an attack (Mathew 1954).

facts.t: Myrmarachne males, with their long jaws, appear to mimic an ant carrying something in its mandibles rather than a plain worker ant.
facts.cite: Nelson XJ, Jackson RR (2006) Compound mimicry and trading predators by the males of sexually dimorphic Batesian mimics. Proc R Soc B 273: 367-372
facts.kp: the male's model seems to be ... a combination of an ant and something carried
facts.note: Cost: the ant-eating salticid Chalcotropis gulosus chose Myrmarachne males more often than females, as it prefers encumbered ants; Portia fimbriata avoided both.

facts.t: Myrmarachne formicaria walks on all eight legs, raising its forelegs like antennae only when stopped, and follows winding, ant-like paths.
facts.cite: Shamble PS, Hoy RR, Cohen I, Beatus T (2017) Walking like an ant: a quantitative and experimental approach to understanding locomotor mimicry in the jumping spider Myrmarachne formicaria. Proc R Soc B 284: 20170308
facts.kp: mimics walk using all eight legs, raising their forelegs like ant antennae only when stationary
facts.checked: read abstract on PubMed (PMID 28701553); species from full title via Europe PMC full text (PMC5524487)
facts.note: Trajectories resemble ants following pheromone trails; also short (about 100 ms) pauses.

facts.t: Myrmarachne melanotarsa lives in silk nest complexes that can hold over 50 individuals, often shared with other jumping spiders.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Nelson XJ, Salm K (2008) The natural history of Myrmarachne melanotarsa, a social ant-mimicking jumping spider. New Zealand J Zool 35: 225-235
facts.kp: aggregations, which can exceed 50 conspecific individuals per colony
facts.checked: read abstract via Consensus; DOI and pages from Crossref
facts.note: Known from East Africa; mimics Crematogaster ants. Nest complexes are many individual nests joined by silk; Pseudicius and Menemerus share them.

facts.t: Myrmarachne melanotarsa preys on eggs and young of ant-wary salticids; Menemerus mothers often abandoned their broods on seeing it.
facts.cite: Nelson XJ, Jackson RR (2009) Aggressive use of Batesian mimicry by an ant-like jumping spider. Biol Lett 5: 755-757
facts.kp: typically preys on the eggs and juveniles of ant-averse salticid species
facts.note: Brood abandonment was higher when Menemerus females saw ants or ant mimics than non-ant-like arthropods or nothing. 'Often' = more frequently than controls.

facts.t: Seven Myrmarachne species jumped and caught prey less well than non-mimic salticids; narrower-bodied species fared worse.
facts.cite: Hashimoto Y, Endo T, Yamasaki T, Hyodo F, Itioka T (2020) Constraints on the jumping and prey-capture abilities of ant-mimicking spiders (Salticidae, Salticinae, Myrmarachne). Sci Rep 10: 18279
facts.kp: relatively lower abilities were found in Myrmarachne species with a more narrowed form
facts.note: Spiders from Borneo (Malaysia) and NE Thailand; a cost of accurate ant mimicry.

facts.t: Neon long stood alone as the only genus of its tribe, Neonini, until New Guinea's Papuaneon was shown to be its sister group in 2016.
facts.cite: Maddison WP (2016) Papuaneon, a new genus of jumping spiders from Papua New Guinea (Araneae: Salticidae: Neonini). Zootaxa 4200(3)
facts.kp: Neon Simon stands alone as a phylogenetically isolated astioid jumping spider, the only member of the Neonini
facts.note: Taxonomic; weak. Tribe Neonini erected by Maddison 2015.

facts.t: Ohilimia scutellata is listed in Australia's golden mimicry complex: at least 140 gold-bodied, ant-like species from four arthropod orders.
facts.cite: Pekar S, Petrakova L, Bulbert MW, Whiting MJ, Herberstein ME (2017) The golden mimicry complex uses a wide spectrum of defence to deter a community of predators. eLife 6: e22089
facts.where: abstract; species listed in Table 1 (mimic species of the golden complex)
facts.kp: All members of this mimicry complex are characterised by a conspicuous golden body
facts.checked: read abstract on PubMed (PMID 28170317); Table 1 entry confirmed in Europe PMC full text (PMC5295815)
facts.note: Listed as a putative mimic only (Table 1 gives 'scutellata (Kritscher)'); not used in predator trials. Check WSC that Ohilimia scutellata is the current combination.

facts.t: Papuaneon, described from Papua New Guinea in 2016, is the sister group of Neon; its Australian species run from Cape York to Tasmania.
facts.cite: Maddison WP (2016) Papuaneon, a new genus of jumping spiders from Papua New Guinea (Araneae: Salticidae: Neonini). Zootaxa 4200(3); Richardson BJ (2022) The jumping spider genus Papuaneon Maddison, 2016 (Araneae: Salticidae) in Australia. Zootaxa 5150(1): 129-147
facts.kp: shown to be the sister group to Neon ... serially down the east coast of Australia from Cape York to Tasmania
facts.note: Second source DOI: 10.11646/zootaxa.5150.1.8. Maddison described it as resembling a large, hirsute Neon.

facts.t: Paraplatoides looks like 'near Platoides', but its author said the name is a random combination of letters.
facts.cite: Zabka M (1992) Salticidae (Arachnida: Araneae) from Oriental, Australian and Pacific regions, VII. Paraplatoides and Grayenulla, new genera from Australia and New Caledonia. Rec Aust Mus 44(2): 165-183
facts.kp: The generic name is a random combination of letters
facts.note: The 'near Platoides' reading is my framing of how the name looks; the source only says it is random. Drop the first clause if the reviewer prefers.

facts.t: Grass-dwelling Paraplatoides have cryptic colours, strongly elongate flat bodies and well-developed, oxyopid-like spines on the first legs.
facts.cite: Zabka M (1992) Salticidae (Arachnida: Araneae) from Oriental, Australian and Pacific regions, VII. Paraplatoides and Grayenulla, new genera from Australia and New Caledonia. Rec Aust Mus 44(2): 165-183
facts.kp: cryptic colour patterns, strongly elongated bodies and well-developed (oxyopid-like) spines on the first legs
facts.note: Others are found under Eucalyptus bark. Zabka considered P. niger and P. christopheri the closest relatives of Holoplatys.

facts.t: Pellenes tripunctatus overwinters in empty land-snail shells; one Czech shell held six together, five females and a male.
facts.cite: Dzivakova K, Fric ZF, Hula V (2022) Microhabitat selection for overwintering: overwintering conditions of three jumping spiders (Pellenes tripunctatus, P. nigrociliatus, and Attulus penicillatus) living in terrestrial shells in the Czech Republic. Insects 13(10): 950
facts.kp: six overwintering P. tripunctatus individuals in a single shell ... five females and one male
facts.checked: read abstract on PubMed (PMID 36292898) and species names in Europe PMC full text (PMC9603921)
facts.note: Authors call the group an unusual social behaviour. P. nigrociliatus also overwinters in shells; females of both preferred shells with more vegetation nearby.

facts.t: Phintella vittata gave the first evidence of an animal using UVB in communication: females preferred males that reflect UVB.
facts.cite: Li J, Zhang Z, Liu F, Liu Q, Gan W, Chen J, Lim MLM, Li D (2008) UVB-based mate-choice cues used by females of the jumping spider Phintella vittata. Curr Biol 18: 699-703
facts.kp: first evidence of an animal using UVB (280-315 nm) for intraspecific communication
facts.note: Preference not explained by brightness or UVA.

facts.t: Females of Phintella vittata and P. bifurcilinea have UV-fluorescent palps; males prefer glowing females, but so does a Portia predator.
facts.cite: Zhou Y, Yu L, Wang X, Li D, Xu X (2025) UV-induced fluorescence in the balance: mate choice and predation risk in the female ornamented jumping spiders. Integr Zool 21(2): 411-420
facts.kp: Predation rates were significantly higher for F+ females than for F- females
facts.note: Predator was Portia xishan. 'Prefer' for the predator = higher predation rate on fluorescent (F+) females.

facts.t: Phintella piatensis lives among weaver ants without eating or mimicking them; mating spiders were safe from ants only with a nest.
facts.cite: Nelson XJ, Jackson RR (2009) The influence of ants on the mating strategy of a myrmecophilic jumping spider (Araneae, Salticidae). J Nat Hist 43(11-12): 713-735
facts.kp: being killed by ants when there was no accessible nest ... access to a nest eliminated this risk
facts.checked: abstract reconstructed from OpenAlex record; journal details from OpenAlex
facts.note: Its silk nests are unusually dense; males seeing ants outside a nest were reluctant to mate. Ant species given only as weaver ants in the abstract.

facts.t: Plexippus paykulli avoided striped prey, yet hiding males' facial stripes did not change how aggressively females met courting males.
facts.cite: Humbel EA, Kimball R, Taylor LA (2023) The role of high-contrast male facial stripes in mitigating female aggression in the jumping spider Plexippus paykulli. Anim Behav 206: 13-27
facts.kp: this aversion does not confer reduced aggression from females toward striped males
facts.checked: read abstract on the paper's Dryad dataset page (doi 10.5061/dryad.bcc2fqzh5); journal, volume and pages from Crossref
facts.note: Striped males did mount females more often than males with stripes obscured; the authors suggest stripes help males in other ways.

facts.t: Plexippus paykulli leapt at flies from farther away on a non-camouflaging background, and stalked more slowly when it was camouflaged.
facts.cite: Bear A, Hasson O (1997) The predatory response of a stalking spider, Plexippus paykulli, to camouflage and prey type. Anim Behav 54: 993-998
facts.kp: Spiders jumped towards adult house flies from greater distances on a non-camouflaging background
facts.note: Background had no effect on jump distance when prey were maggots; slower approach when camouflaged held for both prey types.

facts.t: In tests, Portia africana told 1 prey from 2 and 2 from 3, but treated 3 or more as a single category, 'many'.
facts.cite: Cross FR, Jackson RR (2017) Representation of different exact numbers of prey by a spider-eating predator. Interface Focus 7: 20160035
facts.kp: categorizes 3 or more as a single category that we call 'many'
facts.checked: read abstract (Consensus record); DOI and citation from Crossref metadata
facts.note: Expectancy-violation tests with lures after a pre-planned detour; significant for 1v2, 1v3, 1v4, 2v3, 2v4, 2v6 but not 3v4 or 3v6. Kenyan population.

facts.t: Queensland Portia fimbriata stalks jumping spiders with palps tucked, freezing when faced; the prey's big front eyes cue this tactic.
facts.cite: Harland DP, Jackson RR (2000) Cues by which Portia fimbriata, an araneophagic jumping spider, distinguishes jumping-spider prey from other prey. J Exp Biol 203: 3485-3494
facts.kp: cryptic stalking only against ... lures on which the large anterior-median eyes were visible
facts.checked: read abstract on PubMed (PMID 11044386); the palps-retracted/freezing description is in the abstract of Harland & Jackson 2002 J Exp Biol 205:1861-1868 (PMID 12077162)
facts.note: Cryptic stalking is described as unique to Queensland P. fimbriata (Jackson & Hallas 1986 NZ J Zool abstract: 'used a unique manner of stalking and capturing other salticids'). Commonest prey there: Jacksonoides queenslandicus.

facts.t: Portia labiata detours to reach spitting spiders from behind, but may go straight at egg-carrying ones, whose eggs block their spit.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Pollard SD, Li D, Fijn N (2002) Interpopulation variation in the risk-related decisions of Portia labiata, an araneophagic jumping spider, during predatory sequences with spitting spiders. Animal Cognition 5: 215-223
facts.kp: when pursuing egg-carrying scytodids ... sometimes takes faster direct routes to reach these safer prey
facts.note: Prey is Scytodes pallida (paper: 'Scytodes pallidus'). Only the Los Banos population, sympatric with Scytodes, makes this adjustment; a Sagada population does not.

facts.t: Queensland Portia fimbriata lures Euryattus females out of rolled-leaf nests with vibrations that mimic courting Euryattus males.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Wilcox RS (1990) Aggressive mimicry, prey-specific predatory behaviour and predator-recognition in the predator-prey interactions of Portia fimbriata and Euryattus sp., jumping spiders from Queensland. Behav Ecol Sociobiol 26: 111-119
facts.kp: used vibratory displays to lure Euryattus females from their nests
facts.checked: read abstract (Consensus record); DOI from Crossref metadata
facts.note: Other Portia species and P. fimbriata populations where Euryattus is absent did not do this. Euryattus was an undetermined species ('Euryattus sp.').

facts.t: Portia stalking a web spider moves further while wind or other disturbance shakes the web, masking its own approach.
facts.cite: Wilcox RS, Jackson RR, Gentile K (1996) Spiderweb smokescreens: spider trickster uses background noise to mask stalking movements. Animal Behaviour 51: 313-326
facts.kp: All four Portia species moved significantly further during disturbance than during non-disturbance
facts.checked: read abstract (Consensus record); DOI and citation from Crossref metadata
facts.note: Shown in four species: P. fimbriata, P. labiata, P. schultzi and P. africana. Used only against spider prey, not insects or egg sacs.

facts.t: Watched in the field, Portia fimbriata detours to web spiders kept the prey out of sight for a median 17 minutes.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Wilcox RS (1993) Observations in nature of detouring behaviour by Portia fimbriata, a web-invading aggressive mimic jumping spider from Queensland. J Zool 230: 135-139
facts.kp: Portia spent 17 min (median) per predatory sequence with the prey out of view
facts.checked: read abstract (Consensus record); DOI from Crossref metadata
facts.note: 18 natural detours; median 375 mm covered per sequence. Lab work (Tarsitano & Jackson 1997 Anim Behav 53:257-266) showed P. fimbriata picks the correct route even when it must head about 180 degrees away from the prey.

facts.t: Saitis barbipes males court with red leg ornaments, yet microspectrophotometry finds no red photoreceptor in the species.
facts.cite: Glenszczyk M, Outomuro D, Gregoric M, Kralj-Fiser S, Schneider JM, Nilsson D-E, Morehouse NI, Tedore C (2021) The jumping spider Saitis barbipes lacks a red photoreceptor to see its own sexually dimorphic red coloration. The Science of Nature 109: 6
facts.kp: no evidence for a red photoreceptor
facts.checked: read abstract (Consensus record); DOI from Crossref metadata
facts.note: Microspectrophotometry found UV (359 nm) and green (526 nm) receptors. European species. The same study found an unexpected iridescent UV patch on males.

facts.t: Saitis barbipes females mated as readily with males whose red ornaments were painted black as with males painted red.
facts.cite: Plate J, Tedore C (2025) Behavioral corroboration that Saitis barbipes jumping spiders cannot discriminate between males' red and black ornaments. The Science of Nature 112: 5
facts.kp: red and black males had identical mating success (P = 1.0)
facts.checked: read abstract (Consensus record); DOI from Crossref metadata
facts.note: Control: red-painted males out-mated white-painted males. Pairs well with the photoreceptor fact; maybe use only one of the two.

facts.t: A phylogenomic study found Saitis and the peacock spider genus Maratus intermixed, with each genus paraphyletic as defined.
facts.cite: Girard MB, Elias DO, Azevedo G, Bi K, Kasumovic MM, Waldock JM, Rosenblum EB, Hedin M (2021) Phylogenomics of peacock spiders and their kin (Salticidae: Maratus), with implications for the evolution of male courtship displays. Biol J Linn Soc 132: 471-494
facts.kp: Analyses reveal that Maratus and the related genus Saitis are paraphyletic
facts.checked: read abstract (Consensus record); DOI from Crossref metadata
facts.note: Taxonomic; relevant to Australian species currently in Saitis. Generic boundaries may have shifted since; owner may prefer to drop.

facts.t: Philaeus superciliosus, a jumping spider described from Germany in 1883, proved to be Sandalodes superbus, likely imported in dyewood.
facts.cite: Breitling R, Bauer T, Schäfer M, Morano E, Barrientos JA, Blick T (2016) Phantom spiders 2: More notes on dubious spider species from Europe. Arachnologische Mitteilungen 52: 50-77
facts.where: abstract (synonymy) and p. 67 (Philaeus superciliosus entry, Fig. 10)
facts.kp: making an accidental import with dyewood quite plausible
facts.checked: read the full text (open-access PDF from arages.de); DOI from Crossref metadata
facts.note: Single worn male from the Aachen area, Germany; holotype probably lost. Identification rests on Bertkau's description and figures (12 mm, frontal fringe, white abdominal square). Same passage notes S. superbus is arboreal, often on and under bark (citing Hickman 1967).

facts.t: Unusually for a jumping spider, Servaea incana takes many ants: they make up a large share of its diet on eucalypt trunks.
facts.cite: McGinley RH, Mendez V, Taylor PW (2015) Natural history and display behaviour of Servaea incana, a common and widespread Australian jumping spider (Araneae: Salticidae). Australian Journal of Zoology 63: 300-319
facts.kp: unusually amongst salticids, ants make up a large portion of the diet
facts.checked: read abstract (Consensus record); DOI from Crossref metadata

facts.t: Servaea incana males often court females inside bark retreats visually, as the thin silk walls let the pair see each other.
facts.cite: McGinley RH, Mendez V, Taylor PW (2015) Natural history and display behaviour of Servaea incana, a common and widespread Australian jumping spider (Araneae: Salticidae). Australian Journal of Zoology 63: 300-319
facts.kp: the thin silken walls allow conspecifics to see each other
facts.checked: read abstract (Consensus record); DOI from Crossref metadata
facts.note: Most salticids switch to silk-borne vibratory courtship (Type II) at nests.

facts.t: Most Servaea incana females mate once in their life, becoming unreceptive straight after their first copulation.
facts.cite: Mendez V, McGinley RH, Taylor PW (2017) Mating-induced sexual inhibition in the jumping spider Servaea incana (Araneae: Salticidae): A fast-acting and long-lasting effect. PLoS ONE 12: e0184940
facts.kp: sexual inhibition was induced immediately after their first copulation
facts.checked: read abstract (Consensus record); DOI from Crossref metadata
facts.note: Laboratory study. Males mature before females (protandry) in the field (Mendez & Taylor 2017 Ethol Ecol Evol).

facts.t: Simaetha paetula and S. thoracica hunt like typical jumping spiders but also build large prey-catching webs.
facts.cite: Jackson RR (1985) The biology of Simaetha paetula and S. thoracica, web-building jumping spiders (Araneae, Salticidae) from Queensland: co-habitation with social spiders, utilization of silk, predatory behaviour and intraspecific interactions. J Zool (B) 1: 175-210
facts.kp: are both cursorial predators that build nests and spiders that build large prey-catching webs
facts.checked: read abstract (Consensus record); DOI from Crossref metadata
facts.note: Fact covers two species (S. paetula and S. thoracica).

facts.t: Simaetha often lives inside colonies of the social spider Phryganoporus candidus, gleaning insects from the edges of their webs.
facts.cite: Jackson RR (1985) The biology of Simaetha paetula and S. thoracica, web-building jumping spiders (Araneae, Salticidae) from Queensland: co-habitation with social spiders, utilization of silk, predatory behaviour and intraspecific interactions. J Zool (B) 1: 175-210
facts.kp: Species of Simaetha Thorell often live within the colonies of the social spider Badumna Candida
facts.checked: read abstract (Consensus record); current host name checked on WSC (Phryganoporus candidus, with Badumna candida a former combination)
facts.note: Paper calls the host Badumna candida (L. Koch); now Phryganoporus candidus (Desidae). Simaetha is described as a kleptoparasite there, building its own nest-webs inside the communal web. Observations from Queensland.

facts.t: An Australian Miocene fossil, 11-16 million years old, is a Simaetha: the first Miocene jumping spider described from a southern continent.
facts.cite: Richardson BJ, McCurry MR, Frese M (2023) Description and evolutionary biogeography of the first Miocene jumping spider (Aranaea: Salticidae) from a southern continent. Zool J Linn Soc 200: 1013-1025
facts.kp: fossil ... (c. 11-16 Mya) from Australia ... described as Simaetha sp. indet.
facts.checked: read abstract (Consensus record); DOI from Crossref metadata
facts.note: State inferred from the abstract's comparison with 'central New South Wales' (the site is the McGraths Flat goethite deposit); the abstract itself says 'from Australia', so 'from Australia' is the safe wording if preferred. Preserved even the pharyngeal plate and a neuropile.

facts.t: Tauala lepidus of north Queensland rainforest leaps or walks into other spiders' webs to catch the spiders and insects there.
facts.cite: Jackson RR (1988) The biology of Tauala lepidus, a jumping spider (Araneae: Salticidae) from Queensland: display and predatory behaviour. New Zealand Journal of Zoology 15: 347-364
facts.kp: T. lepidus leapt and walked into alien webs to catch spiders and insects
facts.checked: read abstract (Consensus record); DOI from Crossref metadata

facts.t: Tauala lepidus twitches its abdomen in courtship and contests, and also when it touches other spiders' webs while hunting them.
facts.cite: Jackson RR (1988) The biology of Tauala lepidus, a jumping spider (Araneae: Salticidae) from Queensland: display and predatory behaviour. New Zealand Journal of Zoology 15: 347-364
facts.kp: twitched its abdomen when it contacted alien webs and preyed on other species of spiders
facts.checked: read abstract (Consensus record); DOI from Crossref metadata
facts.note: Same paper also reports females eating each other's eggs.

facts.t: A female Thyene imperialis in Israel was seen leaping into Cyclosa orb webs to catch the resident spiders.
facts.cite: Jager P (2012) Observations on web-invasion by the jumping spider Thyene imperialis in Israel (Araneae: Salticidae). Arachnologische Mitteilungen 43: 63-65
facts.kp: The female leapt into the orb-web to catch Cyclosa spiders
facts.checked: read abstract (Consensus record); DOI from Crossref metadata
facts.note: Single field observation (Negev) of web invasion on Cyclosa deserticola.

facts.t: Trite planiceps lives in rolled-up New Zealand flax leaves, and inside them in darkness signals by tapping legs I and vibrating its abdomen.
facts.cite: Taylor PW, Jackson RR (1999) Habitat-adapted communication in Trite planiceps, a New Zealand jumping spider (Araneae, Salticidae). New Zealand Journal of Zoology 26: 127-154
facts.kp: use vibratory displays, tapping the leaf surface with Legs I and vibrating their abdomens
facts.checked: read abstract (Consensus record); DOI from Crossref metadata
facts.note: Described as the first report of a salticid with a display repertoire for use in darkness away from nests; filmed with infra-red video.

facts.t: Trite planiceps males find females hidden inside rolled-up flax leaves by following chemical cues on the females' draglines.
facts.cite: Taylor PW (1998) Dragline-mediated mate-searching in Trite planiceps (Araneae, Salticidae). Journal of Arachnology 26: 330-334
facts.kp: males use cues from females' draglines deposited on the outside of these rolled-up leaves
facts.checked: read abstract (Consensus/BHL record); volume and pages confirmed via web search of the JoA listing
facts.note: The paper says the cues are 'probably pheromones loosely bound to females' draglines'.

facts.t: Trite planiceps given caffeine kept responding to a repeated visual stimulus for longer than spiders given plain water.
facts.cite: Humphrey B, Helton WS, Nelson XJ (2019) Caffeine affects the vigilance decrement of Trite planiceps jumping spiders (Salticidae). Journal of Comparative Psychology 133: 551-557
facts.kp: spiders were more responsive for longer when spiders were administered caffeine compared with water
facts.checked: read abstract (Consensus record); DOI from Crossref metadata

facts.t: Yamangalea is named from 'yamangelé', the Ipili word for spider; Maddison first collected it on Ipili land in Papua New Guinea.
facts.cite: Maddison WP (2009) New cocalodine jumping spiders from Papua New Guinea (Araneae: Salticidae: Cocalodinae). Zootaxa 2021: 1-22
facts.kp: based on "yamangelé", the word for "spider" in the language of the Ipili people
facts.checked: read the original treatment text via Plazi TreatmentBank (XML of Maddison 2009, pp. 7-8); DOI from Crossref metadata
facts.note: Maddison changed the first 'e' to 'a' when Latinizing so the hard 'g' is kept. The Australian species is Y. lubinae Żabka, 2012.

facts.t: Apart from its large posterior median eyes and spartaeine-like gait, Yamangalea could pass in life for a typical euophryine.
facts.cite: Maddison WP (2009) New cocalodine jumping spiders from Papua New Guinea (Araneae: Salticidae: Cocalodinae). Zootaxa 2021: 1-22
facts.kp: Yamangalea could be mistaken while alive for a euophryine or other typical salticoid
facts.checked: read the original diagnosis via Plazi TreatmentBank (XML of Maddison 2009)
facts.note: Cocalodines are an early-branching salticid lineage outside the Salticoida (Maddison 2009 abstract), so the euophryine look is convergent.

facts.t: Yamangalea lubinae was the first member of the Cocalodinae, an early-branching jumping spider group, found in Australia.
facts.cite: Żabka M (2012) Phlegra Simon, 1876, Phintella Strand 1906 and Yamangalea Maddison, 2009 (Arachnida: Araneae: Salticidae): new species and new generic records for Australia. Zootaxa 3176: 61-68
facts.kp: the first Australian record for the entire Cocalodinae clade
facts.checked: read treatment text via the Plazi/Zenodo deposit of Żabka 2012 (Zenodo record 6170621), key phrase quoted verbatim; DOI from Crossref metadata
facts.note: Same text calls its presence as far south as south-east Queensland ('the Brisbane area') 'rather surprising'; northern tropical records were expected.

facts.t: Three Australian Zenodorus species reared without ever meeting ants still chose ants over other insects and used ant-specific attacks.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Li D (2001) Prey-capture techniques and prey preferences of Zenodorus durvillei, Z. metallescens and Z. orbiculatus, tropical ant-eating jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) from Australia. New Zealand Journal of Zoology 28: 299-341
facts.kp: preference for ants and ant-specific prey-capture behaviour did not depend on prior experience with ants
facts.checked: read abstract (Consensus record); DOI from Crossref metadata
facts.note: Species: Z. durvillei, Z. metallescens, Z. orbiculatus. Preference held after 7- and 14-day fasts. Name check: Prószyński (2017) lists these species under Omoedus; the checklist and WSC use Zenodorus (WSC site was unreachable to re-confirm).

facts.t: Three Australian Zenodorus species catch ants by ambush, by open pursuit, and by gleaning them from spider webs.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Li D (2001) Prey-capture techniques and prey preferences of Zenodorus durvillei, Z. metallescens and Z. orbiculatus, tropical ant-eating jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) from Australia. New Zealand Journal of Zoology 28: 299-341
facts.kp: three prey-capture modes: ambush, active pursuit in the open, and gleaning from spider webs
facts.checked: read abstract (Consensus record); DOI from Crossref metadata
facts.note: Abstract: 'Large ants were sometimes stabbed several times before holding on.' Same three species. Name check: Prószyński (2017) lists these species under Omoedus; the checklist and WSC use Zenodorus (WSC site was unreachable to re-confirm).

facts.t: Ants were 31% of field prey for Aelurillus m-nigrum, yet in the lab it chose ants only when the arena had sand and a stone.
facts.cite: Huseynov EF, Jackson RR, Cross FR (2008) The meaning of predatory specialization as illustrated by Aelurillus m-nigrum, an ant-eating jumping spider (Araneae: Salticidae) from Azerbaijan. Behavioural Processes 77: 389-399
facts.kp: this preference was evident only when the testing environment included sand and a small stone
facts.note: Field diet from 58 feeding records in Azerbaijan; ten arthropod orders.

facts.t: Anasaitis canosus prefers ants to other insects and uses ant-specific hunting tactics even with no prior experience of ants.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, van Olphen A (1991) Prey-capture techniques and prey preferences of Corythalia canosa and Pystira orbiculata, ant-eating jumping spiders (Araneae, Salticidae). Journal of Zoology 223: 577-591
facts.kp: preference for ants ... shown not to depend on prior experience with ants
facts.note: Paper calls it Corythalia canosa; WSC current name Anasaitis canosus (Walckenaer, 1837) (checked via WSC search snippet). Pystira orbiculata (Queensland) is also an ant-eater per this paper.

facts.t: Males of Anasaitis canosus court a mature female away from her nest visually, but with vibrations when she is inside it.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Macnab AM (1989) Display behaviour of Corythalia canosa, an ant-eating jumping spider (Araneae: Salticidae) from Florida. New Zealand Journal of Zoology 16: 169-183
facts.kp: visual displays if the female is mature and away from her nest; primarily vibratory
facts.note: Paper calls it Corythalia canosa. Type 1/type 2 courtship is widespread in salticids, so low appeal; abstract also notes a repertoire of 22 displays including 'flinging up legs'.

facts.t: Attulus penicillatus is one of the jumping spiders that regularly overwinter inside empty land snail shells on Central European steppe.
facts.cite: Dziváková K, Fric ZF, Hula V (2022) Microhabitat selection for overwintering: overwintering conditions of three jumping spiders (Pellenes tripunctatus, P. nigrociliatus, and Attulus penicillatus) living in terrestrial shells in the Czech Republic. Insects 13: 950
facts.kp: regular overwintering of spider species in land snail shells as a model
facts.note: Too few A. penicillatus to test preferences; the three focal species made up 81.5% of spiders found in shells. Pellenes (Australian-checklist genus) does the same.

facts.t: Attulus pubescens pushes off mainly with its long fourth legs, unlike Pseudeuophrys lanigera, which pulls with its third legs.
facts.cite: Goetzke HH, Federle W (2021) Role of legs and foot adhesion in salticid spiders jumping from smooth surfaces. Journal of Comparative Physiology A 207: 165-177
facts.kp: S. pubescens accelerated mainly with their long fourth legs
facts.note: Paper calls it Sitticus pubescens; WSC current name Attulus pubescens (Fabricius, 1775) (WSC search snippet).

facts.t: Genome-scale data show most Eurasian sitticines are one recent, rapid radiation, now united in Attulus.
facts.cite: Maddison WP, Maddison DR, Derkarabetian S, Hedin M (2020) Sitticine jumping spiders: phylogeny, classification, and chromosomes (Araneae, Salticidae, Sitticini). ZooKeys 925: 1-54
facts.kp: most Eurasian sitticines form a relatively recent and rapid radiation ... the genus Attulus
facts.note: Sitticus became a subgenus of Attulus; five Attulus are native to North America and three more introduced from Eurasia. Same paper: X-autosome fusions arose at least four times in sitticines.

facts.t: Bagheera kiplingi lives mainly on Beltian bodies, the protein-rich leaf tips ant-acacias grow to feed their guardian ants.
facts.cite: Meehan CJ, Olson EJ, Reudink MW, Kyser TK, Curry RL (2009) Herbivory in a spider through exploitation of an ant-plant mutualism. Current Biology 19: R892-R893
facts.kp: the main diet of this host-specific spider comprises specialized leaf tips (Beltian food bodies)
facts.note: 'Protein-rich' is general knowledge about Beltian bodies, not stated in the abstract; owner may prefer 'specialised leaf tips'. Vachellia (formerly Acacia) ant-acacias, Pseudomyrmex ants.

facts.t: Bagheera kiplingi was the first spider shown to feed primarily and deliberately on plants, using field watching and stable isotopes.
facts.cite: Meehan CJ, Olson EJ, Reudink MW, Kyser TK, Curry RL (2009) Herbivory in a spider through exploitation of an ant-plant mutualism. Current Biology 19: R892-R893
facts.kp: This is the first report of a spider that feeds primarily and deliberately on plants.

facts.t: Brettus adonis and B. cingulatus invade other spiders' webs, vibrate the silk to deceive the owner, then eat it, its prey or its eggs.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Hallas SEA (1986) Predatory versatility and intraspecific interactions of spartaeine jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae): Brettus adonis, B. cingulatus, Cyrba algerina, and Phaeacius sp. indet. New Zealand Journal of Zoology 13: 491-520
facts.kp: invaded alien webs, acted as aggressive mimics by performing a variety of vibratory behaviours
facts.note: Abstract also lists kleptoparasitism (insects in webs) and oophagy. Same behaviour reported for Cyrba algerina (Australian-checklist genus Cyrba).

facts.t: Two Brettus species solved a novel escape test by trial and error, repeating a tactic that worked and switching after one that failed.
facts.cite: Cross FR, Jackson RR (2015) Solving a novel confinement problem by spartaeine salticids that are predisposed to solve problems in the context of predation. Animal Cognition 18: 509-515
facts.kp: proficient at solving the confinement problem by repeating 'correct' choices and by switching
facts.note: Shared result with Cyrba and Portia (aggressive mimics); Cocalus gibbosus and Paracyrba wanlessi did not solve it. Spider started on an island in water and could leap or swim.

facts.t: Even before maturity, male Carrhotus xanthogramma are heavier, more active and bolder than females of the same stage.
facts.cite: Mezőfi L, Markó V, Taranyi DÁ, Markó G (2023) Sex-specific life-history strategies among immature jumping spiders: differences in body parameters and behavior. Current Zoology 69: 535-551
facts.kp: Males were more active and more risk tolerant than females
facts.note: Immatures of a protandrous species; males also had larger prosoma.

facts.t: In trials, Colonus puerperus never ate the ant-mimicking Peckhamia picata and seemed to class it as an ant early in the hunt.
facts.cite: Durkee CA, Weiss MR, Uma DB (2011) Ant mimicry lessens predation on a North American jumping spider by larger salticid spiders. Environmental Entomology 40: 1223-1231
facts.kp: our focal predator did not consume any ant-mimicking spiders
facts.note: Paper calls it Thiodina puerpera; restored to Colonus puerperus (Hentz, 1846) by Bustamante, Maddison & Ruiz 2015 Zootaxa 4012 (doi 10.11646/zootaxa.4012.1.10).

facts.t: Corythalia conferta has been found living in a potter wasp's mud pot and in a chamber of an organ-pipe wasp's clay nest.
facts.cite: Giannotti E (2022) Notes on the nesting and prey capture habits of Corythalia conferta (Araneae: Salticidae) in urban area. Brazilian Journal of Science 1(10): 37-41
facts.kp: One spider was observed living inside a pot built by the wasp Zeta argillacea
facts.note: Second nest was of a Trypoxylon sp. ('organ tube'). Brazil. Small journal; two observations only. Abstract also notes a tendency to eat ants.

facts.t: On ginger leaves in New Guinea, Diolenius holds its very long first legs like fly wings and walks backwards like a fly.
facts.cite: Żabka M (1992) Orsima Simon (Araneae: Salticidae), a remarkable spider from Africa and Malaya. Bulletin of the British Arachnological Society 9(1): 10-12
facts.kp: the extremely long first legs are held in a way that imitates fly's wings
facts.note: Żabka's own field observation of 'Diolenius and related taxa' in Papua New Guinea, reported in a taxonomic paper on Orsima; anecdotal.

facts.t: Eris jumping spiders drink extrafloral nectar from partridge pea, and plants with resident jumping spiders set more seed.
facts.cite: Ruhren S, Handel SN (1999) Jumping spiders (Salticidae) enhance the seed production of a plant with extrafloral nectaries. Oecologia 119: 227-230
facts.kp: jumping spiders (Eris sp. and Metaphidippus sp.) on C. nictitans collected nectar
facts.note: Plant Chamaecrista nictitans (partridge pea; common name is mine). Seed effect is for jumping spiders generally (Eris sp. and Metaphidippus sp.), New Jersey, USA. Spiders spent 86% of time on plants with active nectaries.

facts.t: A sublethal insecticide dose made Eris militaris personalities about 23% less consistent without changing average behaviour.
facts.cite: Royauté R, Buddle CM, Vincent C (2015) Under the influence: sublethal exposure to an insecticide affects personality expression in a jumping spider. Functional Ecology 29: 962-970
facts.kp: insecticide-exposed individuals showed an average of 23% lower repeatability
facts.note: Organophosphate phosmet. Three authors per Crossref (Europe PMC adds the handling editor).

facts.t: Euophrys omnisuperstes, 'standing above all', was described from the upper slopes of Everest and Makalu, its holotype from about 5,900 m.
facts.cite: Wanless FR (1975) Spiders of the family Salticidae from the upper slopes of Everest and Makalu. Bulletin of the British Arachnological Society 3(5): 132-136
facts.kp: the specific name omnisuperstes (standing above all) ... Holotype male: Nepal/Tibet ... 19,500 ft
facts.note: 19,500 ft = 5,944 m. Name suggested by W.S. Bristowe. Country: Nepal/China (Tibet) border.

facts.t: Small salticids found at 6,700 m on Everest in 1924 seem to be Euophrys omnisuperstes, though too damaged to confirm.
facts.cite: Wanless FR (1975) Spiders of the family Salticidae from the upper slopes of Everest and Makalu. Bulletin of the British Arachnological Society 3(5): 132-136
facts.kp: immature specimens collected by Major Kingston from 22,000 ft ... appear to be conspecific
facts.note: 22,000 ft = 6,706 m; the source of the often-quoted '6,700 m' record. Wanless notes they are 'mutilated and badly rubbed'.

facts.t: Everest's high-altitude salticids feed on flies and springtails living on wind-blown plant debris, the end of a short food chain.
facts.cite: Wanless FR (1975) Spiders of the family Salticidae from the upper slopes of Everest and Makalu. Bulletin of the British Arachnological Society 3(5): 132-136
facts.kp: spiders being the only predators formed the last link in this simple food chain
facts.note: Wanless reports Swan's (1961) finding for the Himalayan salticid community generally, not E. omnisuperstes specifically; fact is worded for the Everest salticids. Card could say 'Euophrys on Everest...'.

facts.t: Habronattus pyrrithrix sees red via a retinal filter that shifts some green receptors to red, a mechanism unknown before in spiders.
facts.cite: Zurek DB, Cronin TW, Taylor LA, Byrne K, Sullivan MLG, Morehouse NI (2015) Spectral filtering enables trichromatic vision in colorful jumping spiders. Current Biology 25: R403-R404
facts.kp: a subset of their photoreceptors from green to red via a long-pass filter
facts.checked: read authors' PDF (Morehouse lab homepage, homepages.uc.edu)
facts.note: Correspondence, no abstract. Text says 'a mechanism previously unknown in spiders'. Gives trichromacy (UV, green, red).

facts.t: Courting Habronattus dossenus males pair each visual display with substrate vibrations: thumps, scrapes and buzzes.
facts.cite: Elias DO, Mason AC, Maddison WP, Hoy RR (2003) Seismic signals in a courting male jumping spider (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Experimental Biology 206: 4029-4039
facts.kp: each prominent visual signal is accompanied by a subsequent seismic component ('thumps', 'scrapes' and 'buzzes')
facts.note: Seismic signals are produced by at least three independent mechanisms, separately from the visual signals.

facts.t: Habronattus dossenus males mated more often courting on leaf litter, which carries their vibrations, than on rock or desert sand.
facts.cite: Elias DO, Mason AC, Hoy RR (2004) The effect of substrate on the efficacy of seismic courtship signal transmission in the jumping spider Habronattus dossenus (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Experimental Biology 207: 4105-4110
facts.kp: males mating successfully was significantly higher on leaf litter than on rocks or desert sand

facts.t: Habronattus pugillis males differ in face colour, setae and dance from one Arizona sky-island range to the next, driven by sexual selection.
facts.cite: Masta SE, Maddison WP (2002) Sexual selection driving diversification in jumping spiders. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA 99: 4442-4447
facts.where: abstract (PNAS) and abstract of Maddison & McMahon 2000 Syst Biol 49: 400-421
facts.kp: divergence in traits of male behavior and morphology ... attributed to sexual selection
facts.note: 'Arizona sky-island' detail comes from the companion paper (Maddison & McMahon 2000, doi 10.1080/10635159950127312): populations on nearby mountain ranges in southern Arizona differ in face colour, setae, carapace, courtship.

facts.t: Sex chromosome-autosome fusions arose at least 8 times within Habronattus, a remarkable number for such a small clade.
facts.cite: Maddison WP, Leduc-Robert G (2013) Multiple origins of sex chromosome fusions correlated with chiasma localization in Habronattus jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae). Evolution 67: 2258-2272
facts.kp: at least 8-15 gains ... of neo-Y ... a remarkable number
facts.note: Authors link this to sexual conflict and the complexity of male courtship. Taxonomic/cytogenetic; probably low appeal for the card.

facts.t: Heliophanus termitophagus eats termites in the wild but accepts a broader range of prey in the lab, making it a 'euryphagous specialist'.
facts.cite: Michálek O, Pekár S, Haddad CR (2021) Fundamental trophic niche of two prey-specialized jumping spiders, Cyrba algerina and Heliophanus termitophagus (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Arachnology 49: 268-271
facts.kp: Both species accepted a broader spectrum of prey under laboratory conditions than in the field
facts.note: Field diet (realised niche) of termites from earlier data cited in the abstract. DOI from Crossref.

facts.t: Heliophanus cupreus and H. flavipes fed a lipid-rich diet survived better and then preferred aphids over spider prey.
facts.cite: Řezáč M, Gloríková N, Líznarová E, Wilder SM, Heneberg P (2026) The nutritional status of Heliophanus spiders shifts their food preferences for aphid prey over intraguild spider prey. Environmental Entomology 55: nvaf135
facts.kp: The lipid-rich diet increased spider survival and led to a preference for agricultural pest prey
facts.note: Spider prey was Dictyna; aphid Metopolophium dirhodum.

facts.t: Hyllus diardi, H. semicupreus and H. treleaveni have all been recorded preying on vertebrates, rare among jumping spiders.
facts.cite: Nyffeler M, Zamani A, Cutler B, Krysko KL (2025) Jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) attacking and eating vertebrates: an update. Journal of Arachnology 53: 143-149
facts.kp: attributed to seven species: Hyllus diardi ..., H. semicupreus ..., H. treleaveni
facts.note: Nyffeler et al. 2021 (doi 10.1636/joa-s-20-090): most cases are frogs and lizards. Prey of each Hyllus species not checked.

facts.t: Hyllus treleaveni is the largest jumping spider in Africa.
facts.cite: Wesołowska W, Cumming MS (2004) A redescription and natural history of Hyllus treleaveni Peckham et Peckham, 1902, the largest jumping spider in Africa (Araneae: Salticidae). Annales Zoologici 54: 579-586
facts.kp: the largest jumping spider in Africa
facts.checked: read title and abstract (Crossref metadata); body size not checked
facts.note: Abstract gives no size; full text would have measurements.

facts.t: In Lyssomanes viridis contests, the male with longer chelicerae usually wins; male chelicerae grow with strong positive allometry.
facts.cite: Tedore C, Johnsen S (2012) Weaponry, color, and contest success in the jumping spider Lyssomanes viridis. Behavioural Processes 89: 203-211
facts.kp: Males having longer chelicerae than their opponents were significantly more likely to win
facts.note: Smaller winners had less red chelicerae than their opponents.

facts.t: Lyssomanes viridis finds its leafy perch by light level and leaf brightness, not by the star shape or green of its sweetgum host.
facts.cite: Tedore C, Johnsen S (2016) Disentangling the visual cues used by a jumping spider to locate its microhabitat. Journal of Experimental Biology 219: 2396-2401
facts.kp: use ambient illumination and possibly perceived leaf brightness but not leaf shape or color
facts.note: Summer host Liquidambar styraciflua (sweetgum).

facts.t: Female pheromones speed up male Lyssomanes viridis in recognising images of their own species.
facts.cite: Tedore C, Johnsen S (2013) Pheromones exert top-down effects on visual recognition in the jumping spider Lyssomanes viridis. Journal of Experimental Biology 216: 1744-1756
facts.kp: Pheromones hastened the recognition of images with coloration and morphology closely matching those of conspecifics
facts.note: Males' template for a conspecific female was coarse; for a male face it was more specific.

facts.t: Maevia inclemens has two male forms: a tufted male that stilts and waves about 9 cm from a female, and a grey male that sidles at 3 cm.
facts.cite: Clark DL, Morjan CL (2001) Attracting female attention: the evolution of dimorphic courtship displays in the jumping spider Maevia inclemens (Araneae: Salticidae). Proceedings of the Royal Society B 268: 2461-2465
facts.kp: The tufted morph stilts and waves from an average distance of 9 cm
facts.note: Grey morph 'crouches and sidles from an average distance of 3 cm'. Each morph won female attention faster at its own distance.

facts.t: Maevia inclemens females carry two separate recognition templates, one for each male form, though both forms look the same size to her.
facts.cite: Clark DL, Uetz GW (1993) Signal efficacy and the evolution of male dimorphism in the jumping spider, Maevia inclemens. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA 90: 11954-11957
facts.kp: females were determined to have two distinct male-recognition templates
facts.note: Abstract: the two displays present 'images that are almost identical in height and visual target area'. Tested with computer animation. PNAS archive is free.

facts.t: Courting grey males of Maevia inclemens are spotted by Phidippus audax from farther away than tufted males.
facts.cite: Clark DL, Simmons LA, Bowker RG (2018) Aspects of courtship risks and mating success in the dimorphic jumping spider, Maevia inclemens (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Arachnology 46: 1-6
facts.kp: P. audax oriented to G at significantly greater distances than to T
facts.note: Tested with animations; grey males also courted less and later when a predator was near. DOI from Crossref.

facts.t: Maevia eureka, described from early-mid Miocene amber in Mexico, is the first known fossil of the genus.
facts.cite: Riquelme F, Menéndez-Acuña M (2017) Miocene spider Maevia eureka nov. sp. (Araneae: Salticidae). PeerJ 5: e3614
facts.kp: This represents the first known fossil species within Maevia
facts.note: Amber from Chiapas; closest to living Maevia poultoni.

facts.t: In Marpissa muscosa the tiny posterior median eyes feed straight to the arcuate body, suggesting they do not detect movement.
facts.cite: Steinhoff POM, Uhl G, Harzsch S, Sombke A (2020) Visual pathways in the brain of the jumping spider Marpissa muscosa. Journal of Comparative Neurology 528: 1883-1902
facts.kp: project directly to the arcuate body, suggesting ... posterior median eyes do not detect movement
facts.note: Unlike the other secondary eyes, which link to the mushroom body. Open access status assumed from bioRxiv preprint 10.1101/640706; check.

facts.t: On a treadmill, Marpissa muscosa needed its tracheae only at top running speed, when they boosted aerobic metabolism.
facts.cite: Schmitz A (2005) Spiders on a treadmill: influence of running activity on metabolic rates in Pardosa lugubris (Araneae, Lycosidae) and Marpissa muscosa (Araneae, Salticidae). Journal of Experimental Biology 208: 1401-1411
facts.kp: tracheae in M. muscosa support the aerobic metabolism only at the most intense physical exercise

facts.t: Naphrys pulex attacks ants head-on and prefers them even as motionless dead lures, without any prior experience of ants.
facts.cite: Li D, Jackson RR, Cutler B (1996) Prey-capture techniques and prey preferences of Habrocestum pulex, an ant-eating jumping spider (Araneae, Salticidae) from North America. Journal of Zoology 240: 551-562
facts.kp: Ants, but not other insects, were consistently attacked head-on
facts.note: Paper calls it Habrocestum pulex; WSC current name Naphrys pulex (Hentz, 1846), transferred from Habrocestum by Edwards 2003 (WSC search snippet). After attacking an ant it holds its forelegs extended off the ground.

facts.t: Orsima ichneumon is a reverse mimic: its abdomen tip and long, mobile spinnerets look like an insect's head with antennae.
facts.cite: Żabka M (1992) Orsima Simon (Araneae: Salticidae), a remarkable spider from Africa and Malaya. Bulletin of the British Arachnological Society 9(1): 10-12
facts.where: p. 10 (remarks on biology) and p. 11 (genus description)
facts.kp: The tip of the abdomen and spinnerets resemble an insect's head with appendages
facts.note: Żabka cites Reiskind (1976) and Preston-Mafham & Preston-Mafham (1984), who say it mimics mutillid wasps in reverse; genus description: spinnerets 'very movable, mimic insect's antennae'. Formerly known as Orsima formica.

facts.t: Orsima is known from both West-Central Africa and Malaya, a split range Żabka thought reflects an ancient range broken up.
facts.cite: Żabka M (1992) Orsima Simon (Araneae: Salticidae), a remarkable spider from Africa and Malaya. Bulletin of the British Arachnological Society 9(1): 10-12
facts.kp: Perhaps its present distribution reflects an ancient continuous range disrupted by climatic changes
facts.note: O. constricta from Congo, Gabon, Ivory Coast; O. ichneumon from Malaya. Author's hypothesis, worded as such. Species count may have changed since 1992.

facts.t: Paracyrba wanlessi lives inside hollow internodes of fallen bamboo and hunts mosquito larvae, pupae and adults.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Li D, Woon JR, Hashim R, Cross FR (2014) Intricate predatory decisions by a mosquito-specialist spider from Malaysia. Royal Society Open Science 1: 140131
facts.kp: lives in the hollow internodes of fallen bamboo and preys on ... mosquitoes

facts.t: Paracyrba wanlessi chooses mosquitoes over other prey in or out of water, even when raised on a diet without mosquitoes.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Li D, Woon JR, Hashim R, Cross FR (2014) Intricate predatory decisions by a mosquito-specialist spider from Malaysia. Royal Society Open Science 1: 140131
facts.kp: preference ... is expressed regardless of ... whether the diet includes or excludes mosquitoes
facts.note: Unlike Evarcha culicivora it showed no choice by mosquito species, sex or blood meal.

facts.t: Paraphidippus cf. aurantius has been seen attacking a bird hatchling that weighed about 4-6 times as much as the spider.
facts.cite: Nyffeler M, Edwards GB, Arkin R (2021) Vertebrate-eating jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) revisited: consumption of geckos and bird hatchlings. Journal of Arachnology 49: 397-401
facts.kp: attacking bird hatchlings ... weighing ≈4–6 times more than the spiders
facts.note: Abstract groups Paraphidippus cf. aurantius with Phidippus audax for the hatchling attacks (Paridae, Trochilidae); per-species detail not checked. Identification only 'cf.'.

facts.t: Peckhamia picata is also spared by ants and spider-hunting wasps that hunt by smell, though it does not smell like its model ant.
facts.cite: Uma D, Durkee C, Herzner G, Weiss M (2013) Double deception: ant-mimicking spiders elude both visually- and chemically-oriented predators. PLoS ONE 8: e79660
facts.kp: Peckhamia does not chemically resemble its model ants
facts.note: Reduced aggression from sphecid wasps and from the model ant; its cuticular hydrocarbons are lower than those of ants and non-mimic spiders. Mechanism unresolved.

facts.t: The ant mimic Peckhamia picata was eaten by predatory salticids less than a third as often as non-mimic jumping spiders.
facts.cite: Durkee CA, Weiss MR, Uma DB (2011) Ant mimicry lessens predation on a North American jumping spider by larger salticid spiders. Environmental Entomology 40: 1223-1231
facts.kp: mimetic jumping spiders were consumed less than a third as often as nonmimetic jumping spiders
facts.note: Model ant Camponotus nearcticus. Supports Batesian mimicry.

facts.t: Phaeacius neither stalks nor invades webs: it sits camouflaged on tree trunks and lunges down on passing insects.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Hallas SEA (1986) Predatory versatility and intraspecific interactions of spartaeine jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae): Brettus adonis, B. cingulatus, Cyrba algerina, and Phaeacius sp. indet. New Zealand Journal of Zoology 13: 491-520
facts.kp: a highly eucryptic, sedentary ambushing specialist that sat on tree trunks and lunged downward
facts.note: Studied species was Phaeacius sp. indet. from Sri Lanka; Jackson (1990) NZ J Zool 17: 491-498 (doi 10.1080/03014223.1990.10422948) found P. malayensis also an ambusher, 'particularly proficient at catching moths and salticids'.

facts.t: Phaeacius malayensis prefers spiders to insects, and other jumping spiders to other hunting spiders.
facts.cite: Li D (2000) Prey preferences of Phaeacius malayensis, a spartaeine jumping spider (Araneae: Salticidae) from Singapore. Canadian Journal of Zoology 78: 2218-2226
facts.kp: preferred spiders ... to insects; ... preferred salticids to hunting spiders
facts.note: Preferences held in two of three test types; some depended on a matching (concealing) background.

facts.t: Phidippus audax freezes at low-pitched sounds, and its brain neurons respond to them from over 3 m away, with no eardrums.
facts.cite: Shamble PS, Menda G, Golden JR, Nitzany EI, Walden K, Beatus T, Elias DO, Cohen I, Miles RN, Hoy RR (2016) Airborne acoustic perception by a jumping spider. Current Biology 26: 2913-2920
facts.kp: Responses persisted even when the distances between spider and stimulus source exceeded 3 m
facts.note: 80 Hz tones at ~65 dB SPL; hairs on the foreleg patella likely involved. Cell Press open archive.

facts.t: Phidippus regius can recognise individual spiders, losing interest in one it has met but re-engaging when shown a new one.
