facts.cite: Dahl CD, Cheng Y (2025) Individual recognition in a jumping spider (Phidippus regius). eLife 13: RP97146
facts.kp: indicating the ability to tell apart spiders' identities
facts.checked: read abstract on PubMed (PMID 41217805) and Europe PMC
facts.note: Habituation-dishabituation test; authors infer long-term memory. A non-social species.

facts.t: Phidippus regius has been recorded eating frogs and anole lizards in Florida, more often than any other jumping spider.
facts.cite: Nyffeler M, Zamani A, Cutler B, Krysko KL (2025) Jumping spiders (Araneae: Salticidae) attacking and eating vertebrates: an update. Journal of Arachnology 53: 143-149
facts.where: abstract (and abstract of Nyffeler, Edwards & Krysko 2017 J Arachnol 45: 238-241)
facts.kp: only salticid species in which vertebrate consumption has been reported numerous times
facts.checked: read abstracts on Europe PMC (2025 update and 2017 paper)
facts.note: Prey (Hyla, Osteopilus, Anolis carolinensis, A. sagrei) named in the 2017 abstract. 2017 paper: P. regius is one of the largest salticids, max body length 2.2 cm. 2017 paper doi 10.1636/joa-17-011.1 (DOIs from Crossref).

facts.t: Moving retinae in salticid principal eyes were first described in Phidippus and Metaphidippus: saccades, tracking and scanning.
facts.cite: Land MF (1969) Movements of the retinae of jumping spiders (Salticidae: Dendryphantinae) in response to visual stimuli. Journal of Experimental Biology 51: 471-493
facts.kp: Four types of eye-movements are observed. These are spontaneous activity, saccades, tracking and scanning.
facts.note: Abstract names 'Phidippus and Metaphidippus spp.'. 'First described' is my framing of this 1969 landmark; owner may prefer 'were described by Land (1969) in...'. Scanning includes torsional rotation of the retinae through about 50 degrees. Dropped alternative: Menda et al. 2014 Curr Biol (doi 10.1016/j.cub.2014.09.029), first neural recordings from a salticid brain (P. audax).

facts.t: The green sheen on Phidippus johnsoni chelicerae comes from a stack of 86 alternating air and chitin layers acting as a reflector.
facts.cite: Ingram AL, Deparis O, Boulenguez J, Kennaway G, Berthier S, Parker AR (2011) Structural origin of the green iridescence on the chelicerae of the red-backed jumping spider, Phidippus johnsoni (Salticidae: Araneae). Arthropod Structure & Development 40: 21-25
facts.kp: a stack of 86 layers ... identified as air and chitin respectively
facts.note: Colour restricted to the dorsal paturon.

facts.t: Phidippus audax can be raised from spiderling to adult on dead prey alone, though survival is lower than on live prey.
facts.cite: Vickers ME, Robertson MW, Watson CR, Wilcoxen TE (2014) Scavenging throughout the life cycle of the jumping spider, Phidippus audax (Hentz) (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Arachnology 42: 277-283
facts.kp: P. audax can survive solely on a diet of dead prey

facts.t: Flies were half the prey of Philaeus chrysops in Azerbaijan, yet 15% of its catches were longer than the spider itself.
facts.cite: Huseynov EF (2008) Natural prey of the jumping spider Philaeus chrysops (Araneae: Salticidae) in different types of microhabitat. Bulletin of the British Arachnological Society 14: 262-268
facts.kp: Diptera ... half of the total prey (50.2%) ... large prey exceeding the length of the spiders
facts.note: Prey ranged 8.1-266.7% of spider length. Generalist: ten arthropod orders.

facts.t: Psecas chapoda supplied 18% of the nitrogen of its host bromeliad, and plants with spiders grew leaves 15% longer.
facts.cite: Romero GQ, Mazzafera P, Vasconcellos-Neto J, Trivelin PCO (2006) Bromeliad-living spiders improve host plant nutrition and growth. Ecology 87: 803-808
facts.kp: contributed 18% of the total nitrogen of its host plant in a greenhouse experiment
facts.note: Host Bromelia balansae; abstract calls it the first study showing nutrient provisioning in a spider-plant system. 18% figure is from a greenhouse experiment, 15% leaf length from a one-year field experiment.

facts.t: Psecas chapoda lives almost only on the bromeliad Bromelia balansae across a large geographic range in South America.
facts.cite: Romero GQ (2006) Geographic range, habitats, and host plants of bromeliad-living jumping spiders (Salticidae). Biotropica 38: 522-530
facts.kp: almost exclusively one bromeliad species over a large geographic range (e.g., Psecas chapoda

facts.t: Its bromeliad host sheltered Psecas chapoda from a wildfire, and the spider population was back to pre-fire levels in 5 months.
facts.cite: de Omena PM, Kersch-Becker MF, Antiqueira PAP, Bernabé TN, Benavides-Gordillo S, Recalde FC, Vieira C, Migliorini GH, Romero GQ (2018) Bromeliads provide shelter against fire to mutualistic spiders in a fire-prone landscape. Ecological Entomology 43: 389-393
facts.kp: returning to pre-fire levels in 5 months
facts.note: Full author list confirmed on Crossref. Fact begins with 'Its' - card can read 'Bromelia balansae sheltered Psecas chapoda...' if preferred.

facts.t: Pseudeuophrys lanigera jumps mainly with its long third legs and needs adhesive claw tufts to avoid slipping on smooth surfaces.
facts.cite: Goetzke HH, Federle W (2021) Role of legs and foot adhesion in salticid spiders jumping from smooth surfaces. Journal of Comparative Physiology A 207: 165-177
facts.kp: P. lanigera accelerated mainly with their long third legs
facts.note: Ablating claw tufts made accelerating spiders slip. Compared with Sitticus pubescens (now Attulus pubescens), which pushes with its fourth legs.

facts.t: The zebra spider Salticus scenicus slows its stalk progressively as it closes on motionless prey.
facts.cite: Dill LM (1975) Predatory behavior of the zebra spider, Salticus scenicus (Araneae: Salticidae). Canadian Journal of Zoology 53: 1284-1289
facts.kp: The zebra spider's stalk velocity declines progressively as it nears its (stationary) prey
facts.note: Also: it turns toward prey seen by the lateral eyes once the prey subtends more than 5.5 degrees, and only moving objects trigger turning.

facts.t: In Salticus scenicus, book lungs or tracheae alone can meet resting oxygen needs, but peak activity needs both working together.
facts.cite: Schmitz A, Perry SF (2001) Bimodal breathing in jumping spiders: morphometric partitioning of the lungs and tracheae in Salticus scenicus (Arachnida, Araneae, Salticidae). Journal of Experimental Biology 204: 4321-4334
facts.kp: high oxygen demands can be met only if both respiratory systems are working together
facts.note: Morphometric estimate, not a direct measurement.

facts.t: Sarinda marcosi is a Batesian mimic of the carpenter ant Camponotus mus; a predatory salticid never caught one in trials.
facts.cite: Hagopián D, Aisenberg A, Laborda Á, Simó M (2021) Morphological and behavioral traits associated with myrmecomorphy in Sarinda marcosi Piza, 1937 (Araneae: Salticidae: Sarindini). Journal of Arachnology 48: 262-271
facts.kp: S. marcosi is a Batesian mimic and C. mus serves as its model
facts.note: Predator was Aphirape flexa (no successful attacks on S. marcosi, n = 15). Study from Uruguay.

facts.t: Female Siler semiglaucus prefer males whose abdomen pattern has lower contrast, judging differences in proportion, as Weber's law predicts.
facts.cite: Kwek BZW, Zhou W, Yu L, Ding G, Li D (2023) Female preference for males with lower pattern contrast follows Weber's law of proportional processing in jumping spiders. Functional Ecology 37: 2434-2446
facts.kp: S. semiglaucus female preference for males with lower pattern contrast follows Weber's law
facts.note: Authors: females used both absolute and proportional differences. DOI from Crossref.

facts.t: Siler collingwoodi is an imperfect ant mimic: its gait matches several ant models and its colours help it blend into the background.
facts.cite: Zeng H, Zhao D, Zhang Z, Gao H, Zhang W (2023) Imperfect ant mimicry contributes to local adaptation in a jumping spider. iScience 26: 106747
facts.kp: a combination of mimicry and camouflage in S. collingwoodi
facts.note: Also had lower predation risk than non-mimetic salticids in assays.

facts.t: Spartaeus spinimanus and S. thailandicus build large sheet webs on tree trunks and catch prey, especially moths, on or near them.
facts.cite: Jackson RR, Pollard SD (1990) Web-building and predatory behaviour of Spartaeus spinimanus and Spartaeus thailandicus, primitive jumping spiders (Araneae, Salticidae) from South-east Asia. Journal of Zoology 220: 561-567
facts.kp: build large sheet webs on tree trunks and they capture prey—especially moths
facts.note: Also: captured moths more than flies, and caught both more readily with their webs than without; walk with unusual palp and leg waving.

facts.t: Stenaelurillus guttiger and S. modestus eat almost only termites, and where they meet they specialise on different termite genera.
facts.cite: Pekár S, Petráková Dušátková L, Michálek O, Haddad CR (2020) Coexistence of two termite-eating specialists (Araneae). Ecological Entomology 45: 1307-1317
facts.kp: At the sites where they co-occur, the two species specialise on different termite prey
facts.note: South Africa. S. modestus mainly took Odontotermes.

facts.t: Most species long called Thiodina were moved to Colonus and Nilakantha in 2015, once Thiodina's type species proved unrelated to them.
facts.cite: Bustamante AA, Maddison WP, Ruiz GRS (2015) The jumping spider genus Thiodina Simon, 1900 reinterpreted, and revalidation of Colonus F.O.P.-Cambridge, 1901 and Nilakantha Peckham & Peckham, 1901. Zootaxa 4012(1) (pages not checked)
facts.kp: the type species is not closely related to the more familiar species
facts.note: Simon characterised the genus from species other than the type he designated. Taxonomic; useful context for iNat users who see old 'Thiodina' IDs.

facts.t: Toxeus magnus mothers secrete milk droplets from the epigastric furrow, and spiderlings drink it until the subadult stage.
facts.cite: Chen Z, Corlett RT, Jiao X, Liu S-J, Charles-Dominique T, Zhang S, Li H, Lai R, Long C, Quan R-C (2018) Prolonged milk provisioning in a jumping spider. Science 362: 1052-1055
facts.kp: spiderlings ingest nutritious milk droplets secreted from the mother's epigastric furrow until the subadult stage
facts.checked: read abstract on PubMed (PMID 30498127); abstract does not name the species, confirmed as Toxeus magnus in Jiang et al. 2024 iScience full text (Europe PMC), which cites it as 'the lactating jumping spider Toxeus magnus'
facts.note: An ant-mimic; some sources list it under Myrmarachne in older literature. Check WSC combination.

facts.t: In Toxeus magnus, maternal care continues after offspring reach sexual maturity, a pattern otherwise known from long-lived vertebrates.
facts.cite: Chen Z, Corlett RT, Jiao X, Liu S-J, Charles-Dominique T, Zhang S, Li H, Lai R, Long C, Quan R-C (2018) Prolonged milk provisioning in a jumping spider. Science 362: 1052-1055
facts.kp: Maternal care, as for some long-lived vertebrates, continues after the offspring reach maturity.
facts.note: 'otherwise known from' slightly paraphrases 'as for some long-lived vertebrates'.

facts.t: Toxeus magnus mothers that raised and nursed young outlived both virgin females and mated females that gave no care.
facts.cite: Jiang C, Wang Y-R, Jiao X, Liu J-X, Chen Z (2024) Offspring nursing extends mother's longevity in a long-term maternal cared spider. iScience 27: 110098
facts.kp: mothers who cared for offspring ... lived the longest compared to virgins
facts.checked: read abstract on PubMed (PMID 38947527) and full text on Europe PMC (PMC11214317)

facts.t: Tutelina similis is an ant mimic that also feeds on ants.
facts.cite: Wing K (1983) Tutelina similis (Araneae: Salticidae): an ant mimic that feeds on ants. Journal of the Kansas Entomological Society 56: 55-58
facts.kp: an ant mimic that feeds on ants
facts.checked: title only (Europe PMC record); text not seen
facts.note: Only the title was checked; no DOI or online copy found; owner may want the paper before approving.

facts.t: Yllenus arenarius lives about two years (up to 770 days), the longest wild salticid lifespan known when reported in 2005.
facts.cite: Bartos M (2005) The life history of Yllenus arenarius (Araneae, Salticidae): evidence for sympatric populations isolated by the year of maturation. Journal of Arachnology 33: 214-221
facts.kp: about 720 days for males and 750 days for females (maximum 770 days)
facts.note: Abstract calls it the longest lifespan reported for a salticid under natural conditions (as of 2005). Dune species from Poland.

facts.t: Yllenus arenarius forms two groups at one site, one breeding in odd years and one in even years, with little or no gene flow between.
facts.cite: Bartos M (2005) The life history of Yllenus arenarius (Araneae, Salticidae): evidence for sympatric populations isolated by the year of maturation. Journal of Arachnology 33: 214-221
facts.kp: produces young in odd years, while the other group reproduces in even years
facts.note: 'no or limited gene flow' is the author's inference from lifespan and phenology, not genetic data.

facts.t: Yllenus arenarius burrows into loose dune sand and spins silk nests just below the surface for nights, moults, eggs and winter.
facts.cite: Bartos M (2002) The sub-sand nests of Yllenus arenarius (Araneae, Salticidae): structure, function and construction behavior. Journal of Arachnology 30: 275-280
facts.kp: after burrowing in loose sand
facts.checked: read abstract on BioOne (via WebFetch; tool summarised, short quote only)
facts.note: Four nest types: egg-laying, moulting, overwintering and nocturnal (most common). Juveniles build far more nests than adults.

facts.t: Zygoballus rufipes males come in two discrete sizes, apparently because they mature at two different instars.
facts.cite: Faber DB (1994) Przibram's Rule and male body-size dimorphism in Zygoballus rufipes (Araneae: Salticidae). Journal of Zoology 232: 191-198
facts.kp: suggesting that males matured at two different instars
facts.note: Females monomorphic. Author consistent with two size-based alternative life-history strategies.

none.checked: Wanless 1988 Astieae revision abstract (NZ J Zool) and Zabka 2002 Rec Aust Mus 54:257 (Consensus excerpt; Plazi has no treatments); only taxonomy and an under-bark record for A. mullion. No WSC access (expired certificate).
